articles.title_zh: Men arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses near U.S. air base in Britain in major incident
articles.content_orig:
Several men have been arrested on suspicion of crimes related to explosives at a village near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. bombers, police in southwestern England said on Sunday. British counterterrorism police took over the investigation.
Police in Gloucestershire said it had declared a major incident and evacuated "a number of properties" in the Whelford area following the arrest of "several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act," referring to the country's laws around explosives.
The authorities also said a bomb disposal team were on site examining some vehicles.
Some local residents were evacuated, police said, and a cordon was established but the incident is said to be "contained."
The town of Whelford is close to RAF Fairford, a base that American forces have used for strictly limited strikes during the war with Iran. After the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran on Feb. 28, the U.K. government allowed the American military to use the Fairford base to strike Iranian missile sites.
However, police did not confirm to the Associated Press whether the arrests were linked to the base.
One evacuated resident told the BBC, CBS News' international partner, that three "unusual vans" appeared in the area near Fairford air base overnight.
Speaking to the BBC, Julian Tubsbery, who was evacuated from his home in the early hours of Sunday, said that "there were these three vans that arrived in the middle of the village and a resident reported them to the police straight away."
Helicopter footage aired on BBC News showed a wheeled robot operating near three parked white vans near the base. However, the police have not yet confirmed which vehicles were being examined, or if they were connected with the incident.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford "remain vigilant" but would not discuss specific force protection measures for security reasons.
"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families," the spokesperson said.
The U.S. military's European Command said it would not discuss specific force protection measures, but added it would "take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families across the European theater."
Security measures have been significantly increased in recent days at the air base, according to an eyewitness quoted by the Reuters news agency who said there had been more roadblocks and armed police preventing access.
A spokesperson for the U.K. government thanked emergency services for acting quickly and added that it would be "inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.
The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine.

More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware.
A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.

NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines.
"Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."
In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida.

articles.title_orig: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.title_zh: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.content_orig:
An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.
Supporters had gathered outside her building overnight on Friday, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received.
Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners.
The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to fierce public anger.
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction, some setting off flares. They carried placards reading “Not one more eviction, not one less neighbor, we are all Maricarmen” and “right to housing at a fair price.”
At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza, some pitching tents. They remained in place early Sunday as dozens of activists staged a sit-in. A model of a vulture, decrying so-called “vulture funds,” hung above the camp.
Earlier in the week, tenants unions and other housing groups held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza.
An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union.
Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation.
“They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.”
Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease.
“We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction.
Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment.
The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing.
The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.”
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing.
Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she is worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city.
“Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.”
Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said she was currently looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs, but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available.
“Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.”
Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe.
“It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News.
It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with  politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.”
“Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”
Jamie Gray is a senior desk editor for NBC News based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_zh: At least 27 people killed in 2 mass shootings in South Africa's Johannesburg, Capetown
articles.content_orig:
At least 27 people were killed in two mass shootings in South Africa's two main cities, police said on Sunday.
The first incident occurred Saturday evening when eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed a bar west of Johannesburg and shot 17 people and wounded 15 others.
The suspects opened fire on customers drinking outside and then moved inside to continue shooting, police said, where they killed 13 males and four females.
The motive for the shooting was still unknown, police said, adding that the suspects torched two vehicles before fleeing.
In a separate shooting at an entertainment venue in a township outside Cape Town early on Sunday, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more.
Five of the victims were declared dead at the scene while the others succumbed to their injuries while being taken to hospital.
No suspect has been arrested in either case, police said.
The attacks come as South Africa, awash with legal and illegal firearms, grapples with persistent gun violence often linked to gang rivalries and competition among informal businesses.
The country of about 62 million people records roughly 60 murders a day, among the highest rates globally.
In March, soldiers moved into violence hotspots in Johannesburg to support police efforts to tackle rampant crime, described by President Cyril Ramaphosa as one of the biggest threats facing the country.
South Africa has repeatedly turned to the army in times of crisis, from enforcing strict Covid-19 lockdowns in 2020 to deploying troops during the deadly riots sparked by the jailing of ex-president Jacob Zuma in 2021.
Soldiers were also sent into the streets in 2023 after a wave of truck burnings raised fears of wider unrest.

articles.title_zh: Ethiopia’s army promises restraint amid fears of new civil war
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia faces renewed war as armed groups launch offensive
Ethiopia’s federal military has said it is handling rising tensions in the country’s north with restraint, as fears grow that Ethiopia could be heading towards another civil war.
In his first comments on the recent military developments, Army Chief of Staff Field Marshal Berhanu Jula said the army was responding to what he called provocations from the Tigray front with “wisdom and restraint”.
He accused Eritrea of funding and supporting armed groups to weaken Ethiopia, describing the “Tsimdo” alliance as an extension of a longstanding pattern of hostile alliances, which he said cannot confront the state without outside backing.
Eritrea, wary that landlocked Ethiopia may be seeking to invade it to gain access to the Red Sea, denied the accusations.
The fighting has spread from Tigray into neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions after seven armed groups announced an alliance , the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, committed to removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
In Afar, the latest battles have taken place around Abala, where the military has been trying to prevent rebels from seizing control.
Separately, in North Wollo, a zone of Amhara bordering Tigray, the army said on Thursday it had killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 in a counter-offensive, reporting heavy losses for the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
The TPLF’s Tigray Army said the federal government had launched a “full-scale offensive” involving infantry, mechanised units and drones.
Abdisalam Balema, a TPLF central committee member, told Al Jazeera the situation had become a “full war”.
Fighting has also continued around Sama, Soqota and Raya Alamata, with government forces reportedly closing in on the town of Alamata.
The army command said it prefers a strategy of “strategic calm” over a large-scale military confrontation , arguing the Tigray front’s popular support is dwindling and its leadership divided.
Internet access was reportedly cut across northern Ethiopia on Friday, a day after the UN said it was alarmed by reports of drones being used against civilians there.
The renewed fighting has put the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray, under severe strain. It comes weeks after Washington lifted sanctions on Ethiopia and Eritrea tied to atrocities from the last war, saying the “national emergency … has expired”.
It marks the most serious challenge yet to that agreement, raising fears of a wider regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across Ethiopia.
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Ethiopia’s president sought to portray the country as a force for regional stability, accusing unnamed external actors of meddling in Ethiopia’s affairs while highlighting Addis Ababa’s role in supporting peace efforts in neighbouring Sudan.
Alemayehu Weldemariam, a professor of law at Indiana University, told Al Jazeera that the federal government bears much of the blame for the collapse of the Pretoria Agreement.
“This war has been in the making for a while now. Much of the provisions in the cessation of hostilities [in the 2022 agreement] were primarily sabotaged by the federal government itself,” he said, citing fuel, service and cash restrictions imposed on Tigray, and the government’s failure to set up the interim administration the deal had promised.
“What was supposed to be an interim arrangement turned out to be permanent,” with Tigray excluded from national elections since, he added.

Before we get to the Week 3 picks, let’s review last week.
The Browns rewarded our willingness to back them after an ugly opener by beating Tampa Bay outright, while the Panthers and Falcons comfortably stayed under the total with 37 combined points.
I'm going to whine about Jayden Daniels getting hurt, because that certainly didn't help our Commanders bet. But I was flat-out wrong about the Packers and Chargers . Green Bay was fortunate to win at all, and the Chargers made me look really dumb for expecting a bounce-back performance.
We leaned heavily on the idea that the betting market overreacted to Week 1. Week 2 reminded us that sometimes a team looks bad because it is bad. We learned from those mistakes, and we're ready to get back on track in Week 3.
The robot is officially on the board! After going 0-5 in Week 1, GPT improved by going 2-3 in Week 2. Both unders cashed easily, with the Steelers and Patriots combining for 23 points and the Vikings and Bears managing just 12.
The spread picks were another story. Jacksonville lost by seven, the Giants got blown out by 22 and Kansas City needed overtime to beat Indianapolis by three. GPT is now 0-7 on spread and moneyline picks through two weeks.
Tennessee Titans at New York Giants, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET
This is what's known as a "plug your nose" bet. It doesn't feel great to back the Giants after they just lost quarterback Jaxson Dart for the rest of the regular season and Jameis Winston looked atrocious in his stead. However, with a week preparing as the starter, I expect Winston to be better and the Giants to rally around their backup QB. Plus, I just don't think Tennessee is very good.
Getting the Giants below a field goal is the appeal, and Malik Nabers being cleared gives Jameis Winston his most important receiving option. My concern is trusting New York to create separation with a replacement quarterback on a short week. Brian Burns, Deonte Banks and Tyler Nubin are questionable, while Tennessee’s running game offers a way to keep this close. I passed because the Giants’ defensive uncertainty outweighs the attractive number.

articles.title_orig: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Araghchi ignores Trump, waits for mediators’ response on Hormuz
United States President Donald Trump has rejected a plan submitted by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, as Tehran continued to insist that only diplomacy can solve the conflict between the two countries.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said on Saturday that Iran wants to make a deal to open the vital maritime corridor immediately only “because they are losing so badly”.
“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine. I’d like to make a deal, too,” he said. But the proposal put forth by Iran “would not be acceptable,” he said.
The plan by Iran, announced on Friday at the United Nations General Assembly, calls for the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift oil sanctions and end its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, said at the time that those steps could be completed within four or five days, clearing the way for the strait to reopen and for negotiations on a final agreement to begin by the seventh day.
Araghchi responded to Trump’s rejection in a post on his Telegram channel on Saturday, saying Iran “will not back down” on its conditions.
“We have seen the first reaction from the US president, but nothing has been conveyed to us from the mediators yet,” Araghchi wrote, adding that Trump had a history of making “contradictory” statements.
He said Iran was “waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators” and would “make a decision based on that”. He added that “only a negotiated solution” can get the US “out of this deadlock”.
US officials had signalled on Friday that Trump would reject the proposal. The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed US officials, reported that Trump was “privately sceptical” that Tehran would meet his demands. He reportedly told aides that he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the US midterm elections in November.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said the Iranian proposal appears “dead in the water”. But he noted Trump has offered no alternative.
“The one thing that has been made clear by President Trump is that he is content to stay in the status of limbo,” Hanna said, “despite concerns from much of the American public that the Iran conflict is turning into another ‘never-ending war’.”
Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway critical to global oil supplies, shortly after the US and Israel launched their war on February 28. Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway have since sharply curtailed shipping.
The US has responded with an economic blockade on Iran and threats of secondary sanctions against airports and companies doing business with Iranian airlines – measures that have already prompted the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Oman to cancel flights .
Earlier in the week, Araghchi met with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, to lay out conditions for ending the war, which would also include waiving oil sanctions and establishing a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was also in New York for the UNGA, said on Saturday that Tehran no longer trusted negotiations with Washington, citing past rounds of talks that were followed by military strikes and new sanctions.
“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera.
He denied that Iran bore responsibility for the closure of the strait, saying the US had “closed the routes before us”. He said the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if negotiations succeeded in ending the war.
Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said Iran’s proposal was intended chiefly as a gesture of goodwill.
“I think they are trying to show the willingness to talk and negotiate,” he told Al Jazeera. “That’s what’s important for their home audience back in Iran, and it’s also important for the American public.”
Harrison said Iran’s leaders likely anticipated Trump’s rejection, since the proposal closely mirrored the now failed memorandum of understanding signed in June that Tehran believes Washington had undermined.
“I don’t think they were surprised at all” by Trump’s move, he said.

articles.title_orig: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Has Critics Raving In Early Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
articles.title_zh: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Has Critics Raving In Early Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
articles.content_orig:
New York film festival: The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects
E ven by the standards of older movie stars catching a major second wind later in their careers, Godzilla pulled off an impressive reclamation of the spotlight three years ago. Godzilla Minus One , the most recent reboot featuring the 70-year-old kaiju – the version(s) from his native Japan, mind, not the Americanized one concurrently starring in a series of Warner Bros blockbusters opposite King Kong – wasn’t just another monster-movie success. It fully crossed over, becoming the highest-grossing Japanese-language movie ever released in North America, and won an Academy Award to boot for its terrific visual effects. Now. Japanese Godzilla characters are mainstream enough to pop up in Happy Meals, and the Toho -made sequel Godzilla Minus Zero is world-premiering at the New York film festival. Arguably the artsiest, brainiest of the major fall fests is playing unexpected host to a truly spectacular monster battle royale, packaged alongside some of the same thoughtful historical context that informed the previous film.
Writer, director and VFX maestro Takashi Yamazaki returns for the sequel, bringing his lead characters back with him. In the previous film, former military pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) used his experience with Godzilla to overcome his guilt and shame over failing to complete a pointless kamikaze mission toward the end of the second world war – the devastation of which brought Japan back to “zero”, hence a newly emergent Godzilla bringing the country to “minus one”. Minus Zero catches up with Kōichi, his now-wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) two years later, in 1949 (although Akiko somehow seems more or less the same age). Another monster threat looms over post-war Japan in the form of a dragon-like creature dubbed Ghidorah, whose menace will be familiar to kaiju fans. (Though he isn’t seen directly in trailers, this isn’t a spoiler; he’s featured from the very first scene of the film.)
Ghidorah’s appearance obviously sends off alarms in the disaster-response agency that now employs Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), also from the previous film. Noda is joined by Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist who introduces less artillery-heavy defense mechanisms for this new threat. Of course, there is a natural Ghidorah deterrent last seen disintegrating into the sea but known for his adaptability – if only the big guy could be called upon and steered in the right direction.
In the older Godzilla films, Ghidorah-Godzilla battles can sometimes make whatever humans who might fit into the picture seem all the more insignificant; the monsters are so fearsome and, in their way, charismatic, that they level anything else in their way. In the tradition of its emotionally involving predecessor, Godzilla Minus Zero grapples more directly with humans’ attempts to assert some control over forces that initially seem impossible to harness. It’s no accident that one of its new heroes attempts to predict the weather – and has faced natural disasters despite her accurate predictions. The characters wield technology that is more science-fictionally advanced than in the previous movie while still relying on a sense of impromptu can-do scrappiness and determination to protect their country. With decreased puny-human helplessness comes greater dangers and new dilemmas.
The film’s version of the US military, for example, is willing to provide planes but not troops to aid in the fight, which is partially how Kōichi and Noriko are drawn back into the conflict despite the pleading of young Akiko. The partners’ skill sets make them valuable assets, perpetuating some of the previous film’s questions about what kinds of sacrifices might be expected or required when sending citizens into the thick of battle. There’s also an element of body horror used intriguingly, but perhaps not to its fullest potential, given the shiver of anticipation that shoots through the audience when it’s introduced.
There’s some value in sidestepping expectations; Yamazaki mentioned at a NYFF press conference that he sought to avoid conforming to any fan guesswork about how various kaiju business in a sequel to Minus One might proceed. True to his word, the movie seems determined to stay true to the human melodrama that proved so surprisingly effective in the previous film, rather than going into all-out monsters-attack mode. That approach works well for the film’s new characters as well as for Noda (Yoshioka is especially good reprising the role), but sometimes falters when it comes to the family-soap parts of the story, which manage to be both more tearful (onscreen) and less (in the audience, though obviously some mileage will vary). The restrained relationship between Kōichi and Noriko made sense last time; in a movie two years later, their nominally romantic partnership seems weirdly glum, even anti-sexual, in a state of co-parenting stasis. There’s little sense of time’s passage for this makeshift family.
That’s not to say that the monster-attack stuff falls by the wayside in favor of the humans. In fact, the movie’s extended climax features some of the most majestic CG monster action put to film; if the fun American MonsterVerse series tends toward pro-wrestling kaiju, Godzilla Minus Zero cross-breeds its fight-to-the-death grappling with disaster-movie scope and horror-movie teeth. Yet it also doesn’t go in for the overkill; like its predecessor, the movie favors quality of visual effects over quantity. Little-yet-huge details like Ghidorah’s lightning-like attack beams have a jagged beauty that makes them both cooler and scarier than so many obligatory effects-movie laser shows.
It’s a fittingly judicious use of computers, given that the world of Godzilla Minus Zero often appears perched on the verge of a post-war technology boom, and on the precipice of the further global disasters that could be invited by the collision of humankind’s supposed innovations and unknowable forces of nature. (Minus One came out the same year as Oppenheimer; was this one, like Nolan’s The Odyssey, conceived in its wake?) If Yamazaki’s previous Godzilla movie ultimately allowed crowd-pleasing thrills to punch through its mid-century anxieties, this one lands a bit more ambiguously. Maybe that’s why the melodrama stuff isn’t quite so satisfying this time around; attentive as the movie is to its human cast, it’s increasingly clear that we’re living in a world of monsters.
Godzilla Minus Zero is screening at the New York film festival and will be released in Australia on 5 November and in the US and the UK on 6 November

articles.title_orig: Avengers Endgame: Encore gets an unexpected Disney Plus release update
articles.title_zh: Avengers Endgame: Encore gets an unexpected Disney Plus release update
articles.content_orig:
The Avengers are in the endgame now... again. The Marvel Cinematic Universe's biggest movie of all time has returned to movie theaters ahead of the massively-anticipated Avengers: Doomsday , both to remind us of the magnificence that was and spotlight the epic tales that are yet to come. And MCU fans are already losing their minds about the presentation of the film and the exciting new footage unveiled .
Yes, Avengers Endgame: Encore debuts Disney's Infinity Vision format while also featuring multiple new scenes that tie the original 2019 movie more directly to its upcoming sequel. As the MCU prepares to close out its Multiverse Saga, the clear-thinking here was that surely a few more ties to the Infinity Saga's greatest offering (and the Russo Brothers' previous Marvel triumphs) won't hurt.
But, in this modern age of digital streaming, not every audience member will head out to the movies to see a major release. So, naturally, some Marvel fans have been asking: When does Avengers Endgame: Encore come out on Disney Plus ? And, perhaps more importantly, will it? It looks like we have an answer to that second question.
Disney has seemingly confirmed that Avengers Endgame: Encore will be making its way to streaming at some point in the near-future. The MCU movie officially has a landing page on the Disney Plus streaming service, which confirms that it will be a part of the platform's library. And, to take it one step further than that, some fans have pointed out that the film is listed under the streamer's "Coming Soon" category in some locations.
While it's not really that surprising to learn that Avengers Endgame: Encore will find its way to Disney Plus considering that it's a major Marvel release (and almost all of those stream on Disney Plus eventually), there were concerns that it might not get a big release considering that it's a re-release (and a lot of those never see the light of day after their theatrical run). Yes, this particular re-release could have been added to the platform with the upgraded color grading, but it couldn't replace the original 2019 Avengers: Endgame as the new footage is specifically designed to promote Avengers: Doomsday right now.
Captain America (Chris Evans) in b/g Hulk (Mark Ruffalo, Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Iron Man (Robert Downey Jr.) and Black Panther (Chadwick Boseman) in Marvel Studios' Avengers Endgame: Encore | Courtesy of Marvel Studios
The fact that it has a separate landing page confirms that it will indeed get the standalone release, with Disney Plus likely treating it as a completely separate movie. And with that new footage designed to tease Avengers: Doomsday , you can rest assured that it will enjoy a big boom whenever it does make its presence felt on the platform.
As for when that may be, the likelihood is that it won't be too long. It is true that the Avengers Endgame: Encore re-release has a real chance of pushing Avengers: Endgame past Avatar - and therefore allowing it to reclaim the title of the highest-grossing movie of all time - so Marvel Studios will likely wish to capitalize on the must-see nature of those new scenes in a bid to drive up further anticipation for Avengers: Doomsday and keep it in theaters for some time. But that still doesn't change the fact that the fans who don't go to the movies still need to see those scenes before Avengers: Doomsday releases in December .
With that in mind, we're predicting that Avengers Endgame: Encore will have a Disney Plus release date set for either late October or early November, allowing the film to enjoy a second, streaming, life and once again build up the hype for Avengers: Doomsday 's theatrical release in December.
Avengers Endgame: Encore is in movie theaters now. Avengers: Doomsday arrives in movie theaters on December 18, 2026.

A new “ Star Wars ” movie is currently in development with director Jon Watts attached.
Watts is best known for directing the popular “Spider-Man” trilogy starring Tom Holland, which includes 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming,” 2019’s “Spider-Man: Far From Home,” and 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” (2026’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.) Before being selected to direct “Spider-Man,” Watts also helmed films including “Cop Car” and “Clown.” Following his involvement with the trilogy, In 2024, it was reported that Watts, his production company Freshman Year and producer Dianne McGunigle had signed a first-look feature deal with Walt Disney Studios.
In 2024, Watts co-created “Skeleton Crew” alongside Christopher Ford, a coming-of-age series set in the era of the New Republic that followed four young characters on a new adventure, per the show’s official logline. Jude Law starred as Jod Na Nawood, with Ravi Cabot-Conyers as Wim, Ryan Kiera Armstrong as Fern, Kyriana Kratter as KB and Robert Timothy Smith as Neel.
With the role, Watts joins a list of previous “Star Wars” directors that includes Irvin Kershner, Richard Marquand, J.J. Abrams, Rian Johnson and “Star Wars” creator George Lucas. Released in 2019, Abrams’ “Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker” is the most recent film in the franchise to debut theatrically.
As previously reported by Variety , Simon Kinberg will pen the script for the film. Kinberg is best known for being a writer, producer and director for the “X-Men” franchise, and was considered a surprising choice at the time of the announcement.

articles.title_zh: Pope Leo draws 800,000 people to central Paris for open-air Mass on iconic square
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of thousands of people packed Paris' iconic Champs-Élysées Avenue for Pope Leo XIV' s big outdoor Mass on Saturday, a sign of the Catholic Church's enduring appeal in the once staunchly Catholic but officially secular country.
The Vatican estimated that 800,000 people came out for the Mass — more than the 600,000 who had registered in advance. The stunning turnout testified to the church's enduring influence in France, despite sharp declines in churchgoing in recent decades and secularizing trends that have emptied churches around Europe.
During his speech, Leo encouraged attendees in a mostly secular France "to build a renewed nation upon roots nourished by faith."
Although a massive security blanket shut down central Paris to road traffic, the party-like atmosphere drew people of multiple faiths and no faith at all. The fervor spanned generations. People brought dozens of babies and young children from the crowd for Leo to caress on the head as he rode slowly past them aboard the popemobile.
"The message of Pope Leo goes well beyond Catholic people; he speaks about social justice, for example," said Leontine Joseph, 42, a fervent Catholic who came with two friends of Moroccan origin who grew up in Muslim culture.
Leo has sought to encourage French Catholics to persevere in their faith "even amid the thorns" of a secular world during his four-day visit.
It began on Friday with his arrival and prayer at the restored Notre Dame Cathedral , the first by a pope since the devastating 2019 fire, and continues with his prayer at the Catholic shrine at Lourdes.
The pope was joined inside the restored cathedral for a prayer service by many of the people who helped rebuild it.
The number of adult baptisms in France each year has tripled since 2016, hitting 13,000 this year. But statistics and experts caution that the uptick, which has been recorded also in secular Spain, doesn't counteract the overall generational trend of children of practicing French Catholics no longer going to Mass or baptizing their babies.
In 1980, there were 513,000 baptisms in France; in 2024, a total of 186,000.
And just this past Easter, according to the bishops in France, more than 21,000 adults and teenagers were baptized, CBS News' foreign correspondent Chris Livesay reported. This was a big jump from the year before, he said.
The rivers of people who crammed central Paris and their joyful enthusiasm rivaled other communal but nonreligious moments of celebration that marked France in recent decades. Huge crowds celebrated on the Champs-Elysées when France won the soccer World Cup in 1998 and again in 2018.
Leo's visit to Paris came as a birthday present for Jean-Claude Farnabe, who turned 63 on Saturday and spent the morning securing a spot amid the throngs of people.
A lifelong Catholic, Farnabe attends Mass in the Paris suburb of Suresnes every Sunday, and has recently witnessed a surge in faith.
"There are more and more converts," he said as he waited for the pope. "Many youngsters are interested in faith and in God. Every Sunday, I see new people, people aged between 25 and 40, who are getting baptized."
The choice of Place de la Concorde for Saturday's Mass was significant.
Organizers said they chose it because it was the only area in central Paris that could accommodate the hundreds of thousands of people expected to attend. Last week, organizers extended the crowd site because they predicted more.
But the choice of the venue has been criticized by staunch supporters of secularism who argue that the site represents the Republic, and that other places such as the Invalides, a complex of buildings where Pope Benedict XVI celebrated Mass in front of 240,000 people in 2008, would have been more appropriate.
France is a traditionally Catholic country, but adheres to a strict form of secularism in public life based on a 1905 law separating church and state.
Many on Saturday didn't identify as Catholics, but came out of interest in the pope's message .
"People are seeing a lot of really terrible images. This kind of event reminds people of what is really important in life," said Thierry Chen, a 40-year-old Parisian startup entrepreneur who is not Catholic. "You see a lot of different people here, so it's not just about one race, religion or nation, but about a common belief in humankind."
Sylvane Le Goff, 68, who lives in the Paris region, came with her 10- and 12-year-old grandchildren to "give them unforgettable memories." Le Goff, who was raised Catholic but is not practicing, said she wanted to open her grandchildren's minds.
"It's not only about seeing the pope but it also is about his message of peace and unity, values I'd like to share with them," she said.
The Place de la Concorde was designed at the end of the 18th century and was among the main sites of execution during the French Revolution. Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined there. For many French people, the square embodies the Republic: French presidents traditionally celebrate Bastille Day there.
Later Saturday, Pope Leo traveled to the Grotto of the Apparitions of Massabielle, the Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes, where he was greeted with cheering crowds singing Ava Maria.
The pope conducted some prayers in French.
He concluded his visit by singing the Holy Father prayer in Latin. After meeting some faithful he left to cheers of "Viva il Papa!"

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said in a technical report released on Friday that an AI model it was training and evaluating broke out of its secure testing environment as recently as last weekend and took unauthorized actions on the internet. As a result, the company said that it is pausing the training of its most advanced AI models for the second time in less than three months while it tries to figure out how to stop these “rogue AI” incidents from recurring.
“All inference for our most capable models remains stopped until we have hardened our systems further,” Micah Carroll, the RSI Preparedness Lead at OpenAI, said in a post on X about the latest incident. The company said the latest incident occurred on Sept. 20. It involved an AI agent undergoing tests on an information-search task. Even though it was not supposed to have access to the internet, the agent found a way to send queries to a public chatbot. The new revelation is significant because it is the first time the company has said that one of its AI models was able to gain unauthorized internet access since announcing a range of steps on Aug. 18 to improve the security and monitoring of its “sandboxes”—the digital environments, usually walled off from network and internet access, in which it tests unreleased models in order to discover their capabilities. Those improvements followed the July incident in which thousands of OpenAI’s AI agents found a way to hack out of their sandbox, with hundreds of them participating in a cyberattack against the AI company Hugging Face.
Since disclosing its role in the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI has acknowledged dozens more incidents in which AI agents it was testing took unauthorized actions across the internet, including multiple cyber attacks, some of which impacted government websites in the U.S. and Australia. It also has revealed that in some of these incidents its AI agents leaked private images from ChatGPT users to the internet. But until now, OpenAI has not reported any activity taking place after July 20, when it discovered the agent swarm that was attacking Hugging Face and moved to shut it down. The company said it had paused AI training in late July for two weeks while it worked to improve its security and safety controls and monitoring. The fact that its AI agents have once again managed to break out of a sandbox suggests that the steps OpenAI has taken to improve security after the Hugging Face attack are insufficient. “The incident exposed a gap in our controls over network restrictions,” OpenAI said in its technical report on the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. It said it was once again pausing training until it has “both validated that the gap is resolved and performed additional red-teaming of the system.”
Asked about the Sept. 20 incident, an OpenAI spokesperson referred Fortune to a section of the technical incident report in which OpenAI described some of the actions it has taken to improve security and control since the Hugging Face attack. “Following the Hugging Face incident, we have continuously hardened and red-teamed our research environment,” that section reads. “Our focus has been broad direct and transitive paths. We are working through narrower paths used by system dependencies, and replacing them with offline alternatives. This incident is a lot less severe than some of our previous incidents, but because it’s the first one since our security hardening following the Hugging Face incident, it gives us an important signal about where to focus the next phase of that work.”
In this case, OpenAI said the AI agent had discovered that it had access to a service called a DNS resolver, which translates between a website URL and an IP address, and that through this DNS system it could send queries to a public chatbot.
It is not clear if the Sept. 20 episode reported by OpenAI represents the full extent of the latest security lapses involving the company’s unreleased AI models. Earlier this week, independent AI research firm Transluce AI said it had found evidence that an OpenAI AI agent may have attempted to hack a cryptocurrency exchange on Sept. 19 and Sept. 20. OpenAI has not replied to requests to comment on this aspect of the Transluce report. OpenAI said that when it restarts training, it will begin from scratch to hopefully ensure the new model’s tendency to engage in “misaligned” behavior—when a model violates human instructions or common sense human values about how it should and should not accomplish a task—is expunged. It also said that it would institute “more comprehensive misalignment interventions” but did not specify what these would be.
The company said that since discovering this latest security lapse it has “added blocking controls at two independent layers, either of which would have prevented [the agent’s] internet access.” OpenAI also disclosed that systems it had put in place after the Hugging Face attack to catch AI agents attempting to break out of their test sandboxes only partly worked. On top of that, an additional system that was automatically supposed to stop training runs once misaligned behavior was detected had failed. The company said its monitoring systems “flagged the [agent’s] behavior within 15 minutes and a person began reviewing it three minutes after that.” But a subsequent review found there had been other attempts by the AI model to use the same method to reach the internet that had not been flagged by the monitoring system. A different system that was supposed to automatically shut down the training run when suspicious activity is detected did not work, “leading to confusion around whether it should have been stopped,” OpenAI said in the technical report on the incident. “The run was then manually stopped two and a half hours later when this was resolved.” Zuxin Liu, an AI researcher who works on “post-training” at OpenAI, said in a post on X that he was one of the employees called in to respond to the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. “It was pretty surreal to watch the model unexpectedly find a way to access the internet from what was supposed to be a super secured environment for human,” he wrote.
Update, Sept 26: This story has been updated to include a response from OpenAI to Fortune’s question about this latest incident.

articles.title_orig: Burnham vows to fix social care after father’s death
articles.title_zh: Burnham vows to fix social care after father’s death
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has promised to fix the country’s broken social care system after his father died with Alzheimer’s disease.
The Prime Minister said that the experiences of Catherine Murray, his grandmother, and Roy Burnham, his father, in social care had motivated him to make it a priority.
He told the Sunday Mirror that the system going unfixed – from his time as a health secretary in Gordon Brown’s government to his father’s death this month – was the result of political cowardice.
Mr Burnham’s father died on Sept 14 , 24 years after Murray died having sold her home to pay for social care. The Prime Minister said that his father’s illness meant he did not know his son had become the UK’s leader.
Mr Burnham’s promise, delivered from his No 10 North office in Manchester on the eve of the Labour Party conference, expanded the vow he made when he took office to “expend quite a lot of political capital” on the issue .
“I saw what happened to my grandmother. You’re going back 25 years ago now. She died in 2002, and she went through the care system, and it wasn’t good enough at all. And that really focused me on the issue,” he said.
“But here I am today, having now directly, painfully, personally experienced the fact that that has happened to my parents’ generation, and not just [my parents], I’m talking about thousands and thousands of people across the country.
“That is a shameful dereliction of duty by a generation of Westminster politicians who have just shown total cowardice in relation to this issue.
“The idea that it’s too difficult. How can the care that we give from one person to another be too difficult for politics? How?
“I mean, that is terrible, that politics has got itself to a position where it’s so superficial and so focus-group-driven that it won’t take on a difficult argument and say, no we have to fix this.”
Mr Burnham is to give a speech at the conference on Tuesday, and is expected to address social care .
Despite not having a “complete detailed plan yet”, he said he wanted to use the speech to “make the argument in a front-foot way”.
He added: “You cannot fix 21st-century care needs on that basis where there’s no prevention and we’re just sending everything to hospital.
“In the end, it will sink the NHS if we carry on in this way. So I’m not going to leave office having done what everyone else in my position has done, and pretty much say: ‘Well, I’m not going to deal with this. It’s too difficult. It’s not a priority.’
“It is a priority for me, and I will face it. And it may make me unpopular, but I’m going to do it.”

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.content_orig:
NAALEHU, Hawaii — Hurricane Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane in the Pacific Ocean over the weekend and unleash intense rain, the possibility of life-threatening flash flooding and dangerous surf for Hawaii’s Big Island.
Nolo was a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 100 mph early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center said, as its outer rainbands hit the Big Island. Hurricane conditions are possible on the island, especially in areas with steep terrain, the weather service warned.
This marks the third hurricane in less than two months to whip past Hawaii (following Lala and Lowell ). The active Pacific hurricane season is likely due to a record-setting El Niño — a natural climate pattern characterized by a rise in sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific, which can spawn more intense and frequent cyclones there.
Tess Kala, a South Point resident who grew up in the area, said the back-to-back storms are a shock to locals.
“Honestly, this is the first like, whoa, what happened? We had a lot of family and friends that have lived here all their lives through generations and never experienced this before,” she said.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said Friday that President Donald Trump approved the state’s request for an emergency declaration to provide federal assistance for emergency protective measures across the state.
Mark Peters, a resident of seven years of Naalehu, on the Big Island’s southern tip, said the damage from the recent hurricanes has not been forgotten.
“It hurts me when I see friends and neighbors and people of this community that I know, and I just see it in their eyes, I hear it in their voices. We’ve been through a lot down here, and we still got a lot to go,” Peters said.
“We’re just getting started with our recovery. But to have yet another big storm hit us, and potentially even bigger than the last one, it’s difficult,” he said.
While he praised his community for its resilience, he said the people are still in need of basics like food and water, and many are in the process of reconstruction.
“We’re talking years. This is going to be a long recovery,” Peters said Friday.
He recalled driving through Waiohinu in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala and his “eyes getting wide open with all the damage, and the cars and houses moved and not where they’re supposed to be, and Waiohinu Park having buildings in the baseball field.”
Kala, the South Point resident, is preparing for Nolo by “moving everything away from the houses, tying things down, making sure that everything is hosed up and taped up as best as we possibly can.”
Nolo will bring periods of heavy rain that will continue across the Big Island and Maui over the weekend, and could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain across eastern and southern portions of both the Big Island and Maui, the hurricane center said.
Nolo is forecast to dump 8 to 12 inches of rain on the eastern and southern parts of the Big Island, with maximum amounts up to 16 inches. Western portions of the Big Island could see 1 to 3 inches of rain, with maximum amounts of 6 inches. Meanwhile, Maui could see 4 to 6 inches, with maximum amounts of 8 inches, the National Hurricane Center said.
The rest of Hawaii will experience smaller rainfall totals, but isolated flooding is possible.
Nolo could also bring large and damaging waves along portions of the Big Island’s coastline into the weekend.
A hurricane watch and tropical storm warning are in effect for Hawaii County, and a tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County. A hurricane watch means that hurricane conditions are possible within 24-36 hours. A wind advisory has been issued for the rest of the state.
Tropical storm-force winds will reach the Big Island on Friday afternoon, with hurricane-force winds possible by late evening.
A high surf advisory is in effect for the south- and east-facing shores of the Big Island and the east-facing shores of Maui and Molokai. A high-surf advisory was also issued for the east-facing shores of Niihau, Kauai and Oahu beginning Friday evening.
Nolo could also spawn tornadoes and large waterspouts over and near the Big Island and to the right of the track of the tropical cyclone.
Marlene Lenthang reported from Los Angeles, and Ryan Chandler and Shanshan Dong reported from Naalehu, Hawaii.

We’ve visited the Overworld, the Nether, and the End. Now, prepare yourself for a journey to the Sift.
First announced at Gamescom and showcased in more detail at Minecraft LIVE today, The Sift is the first new dimension in Minecraft in over 14 years, and players will be able to visit it in just a few days, when Minecraft Dungeons II launches on September 29.
But on top of that, Mojang Studios confirmed that the Sift will come to Minecraft in 2027, offering an entire new dimension for you to explore, survive, and create within.
In the opening stages of Minecraft Dungeons II , players will realize something is amiss. Strange events begin to upend the natural order of the Overworld, new enemy types appear, and souls begin to fly through the world. You’ve stumbled on the Sift.
This new reality brings an entirely different, colorful new look, new mobs (both companions and threats, all unique) and, once you enter, new rules to learn. Shifting tides within the Sift can affect your character and those around you; hazardous new blocks will alter how you approach exploration; new environments will put your skills to the test.
The Sift contains new biomes – including Meadows and Carapace – but Mojang are keeping other areas a secret for players to discover when they play Minecraft Dungeons II .
All of this will get seasoned players thinking about how Minecraft itself will change once the Sift arrives. While Mojang isn’t talking too much about how to access the Sift, or how it will stand out from Dungeons II ’s expression of it, we did get a brief in-development look at the new dimension running.
Suffice it to say, if you want a sneak peek at how the Sift will work, the best way to find out more is to play Dungeons II , which will give us a taste of mobs, blocks, and biomes . And make sure to tune in for future Minecraft LIVE events to learn more about the Sift, and when it will arrive.

articles.title_orig: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.title_zh: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.content_orig:
The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.
With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience .
The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.
According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.
For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World : “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”
An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology , cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.
“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”
Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”
To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.
Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.
Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.
There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”
Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.
For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags , most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.
Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”
But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii ] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”
While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”

Because every Googlebook purchase includes a complimentary 12-month subscription to Google AI Pro, many potential buyers wondered what happens when month 13 rolls around. Will core OS tools like Magic Pointer suddenly lock behind a monthly paywall? And for features that visually inspect your screen, is your desktop constantly streaming video feeds straight to Google’s cloud?
Thanks to an appearance by Google Senior Director Alexander Kuscher on the Android Faithful podcast (highlighted by GbookHub ), we now have official, granular answers on how data is handled, what runs locally, and what remains 100% free for the life of the machine.
One of the standout features showcased during the Googlebook launch is Magic Pointer – a gesture-driven tool that lets you circle or point at anything on your screen to inspect and analyze it with Gemini.
Naturally, having an AI tool that can read your display raises immediate privacy alarms. However, Kuscher clarified the exact technical boundary between local processing and cloud inferencing:
Kuscher illustrated this with an everyday example: checking an incoming email for spam or phishing. As your cursor moves across the screen, Magic Pointer locally recognizes the bounding box as an “email” with zero cloud footprint. It is only when you actively click the element and command Gemini to inspect, summarize, or verify the content that the specific data is sent to the cloud to complete the prompt.
In short: Magic Pointer is not continuously recording or streaming your desktop. It acts locally until you give an explicit command.
During the interview, Kuscher shared an eye-opening piece of internal data that shaped how Magic Pointer was built in the first place: Google found that internal desktop users move their mouse cursor an average of nearly one mile (about 1.6 km) every single day during normal work.
That behavioral insight convinced Google engineers that the cursor isn’t just a pointing tool; it is the single most accurate, real-time indicator of where human attention is focused on a computer. By anchoring multimodal AI directly to cursor context, Magic Pointer can anticipate intent without needing intrusive background screen scrapers.
The other major relief centers on software feature longevity. Every Googlebook ships with a 1-year trial of Google AI Pro (a roughly $240 value that includes 5TB of cloud storage and advanced Gemini model tiers).
Understandably, users have already worried that flagship OS tools would turn useless after that first year. Kuscher put those fears to rest, emphasizing that Google AI Pro is designed as an additive layer on top of the system, not a prerequisite to use your computer.
Much like the “Help me write” and “Help me read” tools on Chromebook Plus, Googlebook’s native intelligence features are built into the operating system at the foundational level and will remain permanently free. articles.title_orig: Two giant pandas on loan from China land in Atlanta and head to Zoo Atlanta
articles.title_zh: Two giant pandas on loan from China land in Atlanta and head to Zoo Atlanta
articles.content_orig:
by MINA ALLEN | The National News Desk
ATLANTA, Ga. (TNND)  — Two giant pandas who are on loan from the Chinese government as part of Beijing's long-standing "panda diplomacy" landed in Atlanta early Sunday morning and headed to the city's zoo. The pandas, a boy panda named Ping Ping and a girl panda named Fu Shang, arrived on a FedEx flight from Chengdu, in southwestern China.
The pandas' arrival at Zoo Atlanta will be met with great fanfare, especially given how rare the pandas are in the US.
Zoo Atlanta returned four pandas to China in 2024, marking the end of a 25-year agreement between the zoo and China.
The pandas departed from Chengdu, in southwestern China, at 2:55 a.m. Sunday morning local time, 2:55 p.m. EST Saturday, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua. The panda's flight came just a day after Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington concluded.
During the visit from the Chinese president, which was intended to address rising US-China tensions, Xi and US President Donald Trump agreed to establish an AI hotline between the two countries.
Newscasts from Xinhua showed fans of the pandas waving placards as trucks that were carrying the pandas headed from the Giant Panda Breeding Research Base to the airport. China arranged for several veterinarians and breeders to remain at the zoo in Atlanta as the pandas enter quarantine upon arrival.
Panda loaning has been a tool of Chinese diplomacy for years, as the government has used them as a cultural icon and national symbol. For more than half a century, Beijing sent the lovable creatures overseas to strengthen alliances, court new partners and mend estranged ties.
“The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans,” Xi said on Thursday, referencing the half-century in which pandas lived in US zoos on loan from the Chinese government. The tradition between the two countries was started by Chairman Mao Zedong in 1972, shortly after Richard Nixon became the first US president to visit China following the Communist Party’s rise to power in 1949.
One of the pandas bound for Atlanta has the same name – Ping Ping, meaning “peace” – as the first ever panda that Mao gifted to the Soviet Union in 1957.
Ping Ping was born on March 17, 2020, has large black patches around his eyes, and is especially good at climbing trees, according to China’s National Forestry and Grassland Administration.
The other panda, Fu Shuang, meaning “double blessings,” was born seven months later than Ping Ping on October 18. She has a small tuft of fur on the top of her head, a slightly protruding forehead and finds food very easily, the administration said.
Zoo Atlanta has hosted several pandas before; another pair, Lun Lun and Yang Yang, had seven offspring there between 2006 and 2016 before returning to Chengdu.

Whistle-blowers were repeatedly ignored as mining interests removed Ming dynasty stones to create a short cut to slag dump, CCTV reports
While foreign leaders and their families walk the iconic restored sections of the Great Wall around Beijing, the ancient stones of a remote Ming-era stretch of the structure in northern central China have been sacrificed for cheaper dumping of coal-mining waste.
For nearly 20 years, a section of the wall in Ningwu county, Shanxi province, was used as a short cut to dump slag, despite whistle-blowers repeatedly raising the alarm to officials, according to a report by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The damage to the Great Wall’s Guojiayao section began in 2007, when an unlicensed miner, Ningwu Chaokai Coal Industry, dug a trench through the structure as a way to dispose of excavation waste, the report said.
In 2013, Shenda Chaokai Coal Industry was established through the consolidation of multiple mining teams and continued using the breach to dump slag, bypassing the long mountain roads.

articles.title_orig: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush, green forest
articles.title_zh: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush, green forest
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG — Ronald Sakolsky never thought his money would go this far.
What was once a vast, dry desert in northern China has transformed into a lush, green forest of 50,000 full-grown trees, thanks in part to a $5,000 donation he made more than a quarter century ago to a local farmer and “sand-control worker” named Yin Yuzhen.
Sakolsky, 69, a retired teacher from Pennsylvania, was amazed to see the transformation in China’s Inner Mongolia region last month when he visited for the first time in 26 years.
“Seeing it with my own eyes, that was the biggest surprise,” he told Chinese state media. “I saw pictures, I was told all about it, but until you see it is when you realize that it’s real.”
Sakolsky and Yin’s reunion last month has been held up by Chinese authorities as an example of how China and the United States, the world’s two biggest greenhouse gas emitters, can work together on global issues such as climate change .
Chinese leader Xi Jinping , in Washington this week for a summit with President Donald Trump , mentioned Sakolsky’s story in his toast at a state dinner on Thursday, saying it “touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between our two peoples.”
Sakolsky was teaching English on exchange in China’s central Henan province in 1999 when he saw a TV news report about Yin. More than a decade earlier, the newly married Yin had started planting trees as a way to feel less isolated in her new home in the Mu Us Desert, also known as the Maowusu Desert (“bad water” in Mongolian).
Moved by her story, Sakolsky raised $5,000, which was many times Yin’s annual income, so she could plant even more. They met in person in 2000, when Yin promised Sakolsky that she and her family would take good care of the saplings.
Earlier this year, Yin launched an online campaign to track down Sakolsky, and last month he made a 10-day visit to China that included an emotional reunion with Yin in her forest, where the trees now stand more than 30 feet high and the government has named a grove after him.
The two of them planted a friendship tree, and Sakolsky collected a jar of sand to take home to Pennsylvania. Yin also gave him a cross-stitch with the words “One Earth, One Dream.”
“I want him to know that I kept my word, and that Chinese people keep our promises,” she said. Yin called Sakolsky her “brother” and said the sapling they planted together would be standing tall in another 26 years.
Reports on Sakolsky’s visit have been heavily promoted by Chinese authorities and widely viewed on Chinese social media, where commenters described him as “a real friend of Chinese people.”
Tree-planting efforts are part of a decadeslong government campaign sometimes referred to as China’s “Great Green Wall,” which was launched in 1978 as a 73-year effort intended to reduce sandstorms and help stave off desertification associated with global climate change.
Away from emotional stories like Yin’s, the campaign has had mixed success. While the Great Green Wall is a “great initiative in principle,” the Chinese government tends to emphasize “top-down, technocratic solutions to environmental problems” and focus on targets more than quality, said Judith Shapiro, who teaches at American University in the department of environment, development and health. The loss of open land for nomadic herding as a result of the initiative “remains a serious blow to some ethnic minority nationalities,” she said.
In the program’s early years, deserts were lined with “fast-growing but water-hungry” trees such as poplars that depleted water tables, though more suitable and biodiverse species are now being planted. “Overall, the Chinese government has done a good job instilling the idea that trees are a great benefit to society,” Shapiro said.
Days after Sakolsky met with Yin in China’s arid north, a likely impact of the changing climate was felt when a devastating flood struck 2,000 miles away along the Nepal-China border. More than 1,400 people have been confirmed dead and thousands remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after the Aug. 26 disaster, which experts say was linked to warming temperatures in the Himalayas.
“I am very, very sad for the people in Nepal and people in China,” Sakolsky said at a news conference in Beijing on Aug. 31. “I know now the world is alive, and if I keep throwing paper on the ground or if I keep letting trees die, I am killing the life of the world, which means I am actually killing mankind.”
The Tibet flood was one of several disasters this summer in China, where flooding triggered by Tropical Storm Maysak in early July killed at least 159 people in the southern region of Guangxi. At least 16 people in Jiangxi province were killed in a Sept. 5 mudslide set off by torrential rain linked to Typhoon Saudel. Researchers said last year that climate change is making such storms in Asia more frequent and severe.
China says it plans to reach peak carbon emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. Its carbon emissions have been “flat or falling” since 2024 and are on track to fall in 2026 for the second year in a row, according to an analysis for Carbon Brief this month by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
While its coal emissions are still rising, China is seeking to fill a void in global climate leadership left by the U.S., the world’s largest carbon emitter historically, which withdrew from the Paris climate agreement during Trump’s first days back in office last year. Critics say China’s goals are too cautious and will leave it unable to meet its Paris Agreement pledge to cut emissions by 65% from 2005 to 2030.
Trump and Xi were not expected to have any meaningful discussion about climate change at their summit this week.
Sakolsky said last month that both countries have common interests, including combating climate change.
“You want the best for your children because you know they are tomorrow,” he said. “You want the best for your country, but it does not mean you have to sacrifice your children.”
Sakolsky called on anyone inspired by his friendship with Yin to “go out and plant one tree.”
“If everybody plants one tree in their backyard or in their park after watching this,” he said, “can you imagine how many trees we would have in the world?”
Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Erin Tan and Fred Dufour from Beijing.
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.
Erin Tan is a news researcher in NBC News’s Beijing bureau.
Fred Dufour is an NBC cameraman based in China.
